body:
From automation to a smart factory

Automation means that machines or control systems carry out operations with reduced need for direct human intervention. A smart factory extends this idea by connecting machines, collecting useful data and using that information to monitor or improve production.

The term Industry 4.0 is associated with the integration of digital information, connectivity, automation and data analysis into manufacturing. It includes technologies such as the industrial Internet of Things, cyber-physical systems, robotics and digital twins.

The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to physical devices equipped with sensors or other technology that can exchange data through a network. In industry, connected sensors may report machine temperature, operating time or vibration to a monitoring system.

What is a digital twin?

A digital twin is a digital representation of a physical object or system that uses relevant information from the physical system to support functions such as monitoring, analysis or prediction.

Consider a CNC machine in a factory. Sensors collect information about its operation. A corresponding digital representation receives relevant data and can help engineers understand machine condition, identify unusual behaviour or assess maintenance needs.

A digital twin is therefore more than an ordinary drawing. A CAD model usually represents the design or geometry of an object. A digital twin is intended to represent selected aspects of the actual physical system, using suitable operating data.

Digital twins do not all have the same capabilities. Some describe current conditions; others support diagnosis or prediction. Their usefulness depends on the quality and suitability of the data and the purpose for which the twin was developed.

Predictive maintenance and production quality

Preventive maintenance is carried out according to a planned schedule or established maintenance procedure. Predictive maintenance uses information about equipment condition to help estimate when maintenance may be required.

For example, unusual vibration may suggest that a rotating machine requires attention. A monitoring system can alert a technician so that the condition is investigated before a serious breakdown occurs. The sensor reading is an indicator, not conclusive proof of a particular defect.

Connected inspection systems can also help identify products outside permitted dimensions or other quality limits. Manufacturers may use these findings to correct a process and reduce repeated defects.

Quality, productivity and flexibility

ConceptMeaningSimple manufacturing example
QualityMeeting specified product requirements.Components have the required dimensions.
ProductivityOutput produced relative to inputs such as labour or time.More acceptable components are made in the same working time.
FlexibilityAbility to change products or operations when required.A digitally controlled line can be reprogrammed for another suitable component.
ReliabilityAbility to perform the intended function consistently.A machine operates without frequent unexpected breakdowns.

These concepts are related but not identical. Increasing the number of products made per hour does not necessarily improve quality. If more defective products are produced, the expected productivity benefit may not be achieved.

Benefits and challenges of automation

Automation can improve repetitive accuracy, reduce human exposure to certain dangerous tasks and support continuous monitoring. It may also reduce waste and unexpected downtime when implemented effectively.

However, automation requires investment, maintenance, reliable electricity, suitable data and trained workers. Connected equipment may also introduce cybersecurity risks. A malfunctioning sensor or incorrect programme can cause repeated production errors.

Workforce transition and Indian initiatives

Automation changes the kinds of work performed in factories. Some repetitive tasks may be reduced, while demand can increase for technicians who operate, maintain, programme and inspect advanced equipment. Retraining and skill development are therefore important parts of industrial modernisation.

SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 is an initiative of the Ministry of Heavy Industries that promotes awareness, demonstration, training and support for advanced manufacturing technologies. In an official statement dated 20 December 2024, the ministry identified 4 established SAMARTH centres: IIT Delhi, C4i4 Pune, IISc Bengaluru and the Central Manufacturing Technology Institute in Bengaluru. This was the ministry's reported position on that date, not a claim that the number could never change.

Prelims focus

  • Industry 4.0 connects manufacturing with digital systems, data and automation.
  • IoT devices can collect and exchange information through networks.
  • A digital twin uses relevant information from a physical system.
  • Predictive maintenance uses equipment-condition information; preventive maintenance follows a planned approach.
  • SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 is associated with the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
  • Trap: A static digital drawing is not automatically a functioning digital twin.

[Sources: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Kibira and Shao, Data Requirements for a Digital Twin of a CNC Machine Tool, abstract, published 29 January 2026, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Heavy Industries, Press Information Bureau, Samarth Udyog Bharat 4.0, parliamentary reply, 20 December 2024, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Industries, printed pp. 50–52.]

pictures.caption: Operating data connects a physical machine with its digital twin and supports informed decisions.

title: Digital Twins, Smart Factories, Productivity and Workforce Transition

body:
What makes a mineral critical?

A critical mineral is a mineral or mineral-derived material considered important for a country's economy, essential industries or strategic requirements, particularly when its supply faces significant risks.

Criticality depends on more than geological scarcity. A mineral may be available in the Earth's crust but still pose a supply risk if economically usable deposits are concentrated in a few places or if refining capacity is controlled by a small number of suppliers.

Mineral criticality reflects the combination of a material's importance for essential uses and the risk that its supply may be disrupted or insufficient.

Critical-mineral lists are usually prepared for particular countries or policy purposes. They can differ because countries have different industries, resources and trade dependencies. A material's critical status can also change over time.

Mineral, ore, resource and reserve

These terms describe related but different ideas.

  • Mineral: A naturally occurring substance with characteristic chemical composition and physical properties.
  • Ore: A natural material containing valuable constituents that can be economically extracted under relevant conditions.
  • Mineral resource: A concentration of material of potential economic interest, identified with an appropriate degree of geological evidence.
  • Mineral reserve: The economically mineable portion of a suitable mineral resource, established after considering relevant technical, economic and other factors.

All economically mineable reserves are related to identified resources, but not every identified resource is an economically mineable reserve. An announcement of mineral exploration does not mean that commercial production has started.

Which minerals are important for modern technologies?

Mineral or groupImportant applicationUseful distinction
LithiumRechargeable lithium-ion batteries.Lithium is not a rare earth element.
CobaltSelected rechargeable battery cathodes and specialised alloys.Not used in every battery chemistry.
NickelStainless steel, alloys and selected battery cathodes.Has important uses beyond batteries.
Natural graphiteBattery anodes and industrial applications.Graphite is a non-metallic form of carbon.
Rare earth elementsSelected permanent magnets, electronics and other advanced materials.A group of elements, not a single mineral.
CopperElectrical wiring, motors, transformers and power networks.Valued for electrical conductivity.
GalliumCertain semiconductor materials and electronic devices.Often recovered during the processing of other metals.

Critical minerals and rare earth elements are not synonyms

Rare earth elements (REEs) are a group of 17 elements: the 15 lanthanides, together with scandium and yttrium.

Neodymium and dysprosium are examples relevant to some high-performance permanent magnets. Such magnets can be used in selected electric motors and wind-power equipment.

However, lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper and graphite are not rare earth elements. They may be strategically important without belonging to the rare earth group.

The word rare can also be misleading. Several rare earth elements are not exceptionally scarce in the Earth's crust; obtaining concentrated, commercially useful and separated products can be difficult.

Where important mineral supplies are concentrated

Mineral deposits are unevenly distributed because they form under particular geological conditions. Their location influences mining, industrial development and international trade.

  • Democratic Republic of the Congo: A major source of mined cobalt.
  • Australia: An important producer of mined lithium.
  • South America: Important lithium resources and production, including extraction from suitable brine deposits.
  • Indonesia: A major centre of nickel production and refining.
  • China: A major centre for processing and refining several minerals used in energy and advanced technologies.

These are broad supply-chain associations, not a complete list of producing countries or a claim that each country has a monopoly. Mining and refining may also occur in different countries.

Prelims focus

  • Criticality involves both strategic or economic importance and supply risk.
  • A resource is not automatically an economically mineable reserve.
  • Rare earth elements comprise 17 elements: 15 lanthanides, scandium and yttrium.
  • Lithium and graphite are not rare earth elements.
  • The Democratic Republic of the Congo is important for cobalt; Australia is important for lithium; Indonesia is important for nickel.
  • Trap: A large geological occurrence does not by itself establish a working commercial mine.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 24–26; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 72–76; U.S. Geological Survey, Rare Earths Statistics and Information, section Rare Earths Insights and Data, consulted 14 November 2026; International Energy Agency, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, Executive Summary and Outlook, published 16 July 2026, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Mines, Press Information Bureau, Thirty Minerals Listed as Critical Minerals for India, 11 December 2023, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Workers in protective equipment observe a rock conveyor leading from an Indian mine and stockpiles toward a processing facility.
pictures.caption: Mineral extraction begins the supply chain for many industrial materials.

pictures.alt: Mineral criticality combines economic importance and supply risk, may vary by country and time, and is not determined by physical rarity alone.
pictures.caption: A mineral becomes critical because of its importance and the vulnerability of its supply.

title: Critical Minerals: Meaning, Important Uses and Global Distribution

body:
A mineral deposit is only the beginning of the supply chain

Modern industries usually require processed materials rather than untreated rock. Therefore, the security of a mineral supply depends on several stages between the deposit and the finished product.

The main stages can be understood in the following order:

  1. Exploration: Geological investigations identify and evaluate possible mineral deposits.
  2. Mining or extraction: Mineral-bearing material is removed from the ground or recovered from another natural source.
  3. Beneficiation: Useful mineral constituents are concentrated by separating them from unwanted material.
  4. Processing and refining: Minerals are converted into materials of the quality or purity needed by industry.
  5. Component manufacturing: Refined materials are made into battery materials, magnets, electronic components, alloys or other industrial products.
  6. Final use: Components become part of vehicles, electrical equipment, machinery and other products.

At the end of a product's useful life, suitable material may be recovered and returned to the supply chain through recycling.

Mining concentration and refining concentration

It is important to distinguish the country where a mineral is mined from the country where it is processed or refined.

For example, one country may extract mineral-bearing material and export it to another country for refining. The refined product may then be exported again for manufacturing batteries, motors or electronic components.

This creates different kinds of supply dependency. A country can possess mineral deposits but still rely on imported refining services. Another country may have relatively limited deposits yet hold a strong position in the processing industry.

What recent international evidence shows

The International Energy Agency's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, published on 16 July 2026, reported that the refining of several important minerals remained highly concentrated.

For the minerals examined in its refining-concentration comparison, excluding rare earths, the average market share of the largest refining country increased from 70% in 2023 to 72% in 2025. The agency identified Indonesia as the leading refiner for nickel and China as the leading refiner for several other key energy minerals.

These figures describe an average of leading-country shares across the specified mineral markets. They do not mean that one country refined 72% of every critical mineral or that 72% of all minerals worldwide came from a single source.

Why concentrated supply can create insecurity

  • Trade disruption: Export restrictions or transport problems can interrupt supplies.
  • Price volatility: A sudden shortage can increase prices for manufacturers.
  • Processing dependence: Having ore does not guarantee access to battery-grade or electronics-grade material.
  • Long development periods: New mining and processing facilities can take considerable time to establish.
  • By-product dependence: Some important materials are recovered mainly during the production of other metals, limiting how quickly their supply can increase independently.

For example, gallium is commonly recovered in connection with the processing of other mineral commodities. Increasing demand for gallium does not automatically produce a corresponding increase in supply.

Recycling as a source of mineral security

Recycling recovers useful materials from manufacturing waste or products that have reached the end of their useful life. Copper can be recovered from suitable electrical scrap, while used batteries may contain recoverable lithium, nickel and cobalt, depending on their chemistry.

Recycling can reduce the need for newly mined material, lessen waste and diversify supply. However, recycling requires collection, sorting, processing and quality control. Some products are difficult to dismantle, and recovery may involve material losses.

Recycling does not eliminate the need for mining. When demand is growing rapidly, the quantity available from discarded products may be too small to supply all new manufacturing requirements.

Substitution and efficient material use

Substitution means replacing a material with another material or technology that performs the required function.

For instance, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries do not require nickel or cobalt in their cathode material. They still contain lithium. Sodium-ion batteries may reduce lithium requirements in suitable applications, but they are not automatically preferable for every use.

Other approaches include designing products to need less of a scarce material, developing alternative components and improving manufacturing efficiency. Substitution may be limited by performance, cost, safety and the availability of the substitute material itself.

Building a resilient supply chain

Countries can improve material security through domestic exploration, processing capacity, imports from different suppliers, international cooperation, recycling, substitution and suitable stockpiling arrangements. Each measure addresses a different source of risk.

Prelims focus

  • Beneficiation concentrates useful mineral material; refining produces materials suitable for further industrial use.
  • Mining and refining can be concentrated in different countries.
  • The IEA's 2026 report gave a 72% average leading-country refining share for the selected markets excluding rare earths, using 2025 data.
  • Recycling is a secondary source of minerals.
  • LFP battery cathodes do not require nickel or cobalt but still use lithium.
  • Trap: Mineral-rich countries are not necessarily self-sufficient in mineral processing or advanced component manufacturing.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Industries, printed pp. 50–52; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 72–76, and Manufacturing Industries, printed pp. 85–86; International Energy Agency, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026, Executive Summary and Outlook, published 16 July 2026, refining data for 2023 and 2025, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Mines, Press Information Bureau, Cabinet Approves National Critical Mineral Mission, section on the mineral value chain, 29 January 2025, consulted 14 November 2026.]
